-

A student's contribution enters classroom inquiry through judgments about what the response means and whether it deserves further attention. In an example discussed by Cowie and colleagues, a teacher dismissed an unexpected answer before hearing the students' reasoning about how animals could be compared (Cowie et al., 2018). Such moments bring into focus what teachers notice and how they respond as students develop scientific ideas (Krist et al., 2023). The question of students' epistemic agency extends beyond recognition of an idea to their opportunities to influence the problem being investigated and the work undertaken in response (Miller et al., 2018; Stroupe, 2014).

-

Those opportunities are shaped by planning as well as by decisions made during inquiry. Opening curricula to students' contributions creates possibilities for epistemic agency, while sustaining an investigation requires disciplinary support and resources (Ko & Krist, 2019; DeCoito, 2024). The tension becomes apparent when students pursue a phenomenon in ways that unsettle an anticipated sequence. In a Grade 6 flight investigation, their work with materials challenged activities the teacher had prepared for knowledge building (Reeve, 2023). A responsive curriculum therefore depends on how teachers make room for emerging questions while maintaining opportunities to develop scientifically adequate explanations.

-

Influence over a project's topic can coexist with unequal influence over what happens within it. In a Grade 7 Science and Technology project, students chose to investigate Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls and prepared a public Red Dress exhibition, while some reported that peers overlooked their ideas during collaboration (Jao et al., 2026). Questions about participation emerge at another point in an inquiry when students and adults negotiate the standards guiding a decision. During a seventh-grade biology investigation, students' concerns about upsetting community survey respondents contributed to deliberations about responsible evidence gathering (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2026). Taken together, the cases distinguish opportunities to choose an inquiry direction from opportunities to influence its conduct and criteria.

-

The criteria themselves are a form of classroom authority. Productive disciplinary engagement links students' authority to their responsibilities within a shared problem and the resources available to investigate it (Engle & Conant, 2002). Rightful presence raises questions about the historically unequal conditions under which particular contributions, relationships, and challenges to established practices can be recognized (Calabrese Barton & Tan, 2020). These perspectives extend the distinction emerging from the classroom cases. Participation concerns the intellectual work students can undertake, including whether the grounds for judging that work are themselves open to discussion.

-

What teachers attend to together also shapes the judgments they bring back to classrooms. Sustained professional learning has supported science teachers' attention to students' epistemic practices, while collaborative development of instructional materials offers another setting for examining practice (Shim & Thompson, 2022; Jao & McDougall, 2015). Yet collaboration does not make every aspect of teaching equally available for scrutiny. In rehearsals of mathematical defining, discussion concentrated on pedagogical approaches, with relatively few opportunities to consider students' reasoning about definitions (Kobiela et al., 2023). The focus of professional dialogue matters when considering how teachers learn to interpret students' ideas and how those interpretations enter subsequent decisions.

-

An unexpected student question brings these concerns into a single classroom moment. The teacher must consider the explanation's disciplinary adequacy and decide what the class will investigate next. How that judgment is articulated, and whether the student can question its grounds, reveals the authority exercised through ordinary decisions about inquiry.

+

A student's contribution becomes evidence of scientific reasoning through the questions a teacher asks and the interpretation that follows. In an example discussed by Cowie and colleagues, a teacher dismissed an unexpected answer before hearing the students' reasoning, which drew on a different way of comparing the animals in the task (Cowie et al., 2018). Research on teacher noticing examines how teachers attend to students' ideas and respond during science discussions (Krist et al., 2023). These accounts show how a contribution may enter or disappear from collective consideration. Epistemic agency extends the question to students' opportunities to influence what the class investigates (Miller et al., 2018; Stroupe, 2014).

+

Teachers also establish some of these opportunities before a lesson begins. A curriculum can invite students to shape investigations and the representations used to explain phenomena (Ko & Krist, 2019). Such invitations still depend on the disciplinary resources available when students pursue an unexpected question. Planning inquiry-oriented STEM teaching requires attention to the disciplinary support students may need (DeCoito, 2024). In a Grade 6 flight investigation, students' work with physical materials challenged the activities initially prepared for knowledge building (Reeve, 2023). Planning also involves deciding how students can pursue an unexpected direction with the time and resources available. That decision affects which questions can become part of the class's scientific work.

+

Students' influence may also differ across the decisions within an inquiry. In a Grade 7 Science and Technology project, students chose to investigate Missing and Murdered Indigenous Women and Girls and developed a public Red Dress exhibition. Their sense of ownership coexisted with accounts of peers overlooking some ideas during collaboration (Jao et al., 2026). In another Grade 7 classroom, concerns about how a community survey might affect respondents became part of the criteria students and adults used to judge a responsible investigation (Krishnamoorthy et al., 2026). Choosing an inquiry topic offers one form of influence. As the work develops, the authority to determine what counts as a responsible investigation may be negotiated again. The two cases bring those later decisions into view, including whether students' concerns can change the criteria guiding the work.

+

Authority is also shaped by what the classroom recognizes as legitimate knowledge and action. Productive disciplinary engagement connects student authority with responsibility to peers and access to resources for investigating a problem (Engle & Conant, 2002). Rightful presence brings a further concern into view, asking how historically unequal relations shape whose ways of knowing are recognized and whose challenges to classroom norms can have consequences (Calabrese Barton & Tan, 2020). The authority exercised through disciplinary standards can be less visible than the choices students make among activities. Participation also depends on whether students can question the criteria by which their explanations are judged.

+

Collaborative professional learning can develop teachers' attention to students' epistemic practices (Shim & Thompson, 2022) and create opportunities to design instructional materials together (Jao & McDougall, 2015). The focus of that work also shapes what becomes available for reconsideration. In rehearsals of mathematical defining, prospective teachers and teacher educators concentrated on pedagogical issues, with few opportunities to discuss students' reasoning about definitions (Kobiela et al., 2023). This emphasis shows how opportunities to examine students' disciplinary thinking can remain limited even in activities designed to support teachers' learning.

+

An unexpected student question can bring disciplinary evaluation and classroom authority into the same interaction. The teacher considers the scientific explanation involved while deciding how the lesson might proceed. The grounds offered for that decision, and students' opportunities to respond, shape whether the question becomes part of the class's inquiry.
